title: Cîteaux (1098)
hook: monks seek a simpler, stricter Benedictine life in white habits

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anselm, the monk who called his book faith seeking understanding. Your line was faith seeking understanding. Today, monks who decided they wanted less.

An iron candlestick. A cross of painted wood, not gold. Walls of bare stone, and light coming in through plain glass. Stand in an old Cistercian church and the first thing you may notice is what isn't there. No crowd of carved monsters on the columns. No silver on the altar. Just stone, light, and the sound of a few voices singing psalms. The builders chose less, on purpose.
screen: `AN IRON CANDLESTICK.` → `WHAT ISN'T THERE.` → `LESS, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: It began with a leaving. Robert, abbot of a monastery called Molesme, came to think that he and his monks weren't keeping the Rule of Saint Benedict as it was written. So he left with a group of brothers and founded what the early accounts simply call the New Monastery, in a wild, lonely place called Cîteaux. Their own early account says they set aside whatever they couldn't find in the Rule: fur garments, undershirts, extra dishes at table. They went back to working the land with their own hands, in habits of undyed wool, which is why people came to call them the white monks. Early Cistercian rules ask for crosses of painted wood, not gold or silver, and candlesticks of iron. The aim wasn't ugliness. It was attention: nothing in the room competing with prayer. One of the early abbots, Stephen Harding, is credited with a Charter of Charity linking the new houses, so they kept one way of life and looked after one another. Cluny and Cîteaux both followed Benedict, and the Church honors saints from each; they heard the same Rule in different keys. Jesus says to Martha, in the Douay-Rheims: "thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary." Some readers hear the whole Cistercian plan in that sentence: plainer.
screen: `LEAVING FOR THE NEW MONASTERY.` · `CUT WHAT ISN'T IN THE RULE.` · `PAINTED WOOD, IRON, PLAIN GLASS.` · `A CHARTER OF CHARITY.` · then, large: `PLAINER.`

segments.voice: Look around the room you're in and find one thing that crowds out what matters: a cluttered corner, an app you open without meaning to, a commitment kept out of habit. Don't fix it; just see it plainly, and feel the space it would leave. If you pray, rest in Jesus's words to Martha: one thing is necessary.
Cistercian. A monk or nun of the way of life born at Cîteaux: the Rule of Benedict kept closely, in undyed wool, with plain churches and work of the hands. Today's word.
Your line: plainer. Less in the room can leave more room for what matters. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Cistercian monks and nuns, including the Trappists, still live by the Rule of Saint Benedict with manual work, silence and the hours of prayer, and their abbey churches are kept plain; some abbeys welcome guests for retreats.

notes: Exordium Parvum paraphrased: Robert of Molesme and brothers leave to keep the Rule more purely; the 'New Monastery'; rejection of what is not in the Rule (cowls of fur, shirts, extra dishes, etc.); manual labor. Confirm items listed.
Painted wooden crosses and iron candlesticks: from early Cistercian statutes (often cited from the Exordium Parvum ch. 17 / Instituta). Confirm source and wording.
'The white monks' for undyed habits: general; confirm.
Carta Caritatis attributed to Stephen Harding; the dates in the title and the annual general chapter are left unvoiced under the claims rule.

Cluny and Cîteaux framed as two ways of hearing the same Rule, without ranking; Bernard's Apologia critique of ornament (carved monsters) is alluded to in the hook only as 'no crowd of carved monsters on the columns'. Confirm fairness.
